### Dive into [[Markdown]] > Inline code and code blocks

## Inline code and code blocks
What if you want to write a filename, or a bit of code? Put a backtick on either side:

```markdown
The first photo is `IMG_0001.jpg`.
```

You’ll see the filename formatted like this: `IMG_0001.jpg`.

For several lines, use three backticks on a line of their own to start and end a code block. Let’s try a little JavaScript:

````markdown
```javascript
const destination = "the riverside"
console.log(`Let’s take some photos at ${destination}!`)
```
````

The `javascript` after the opening backticks tells SilverBullet which language we’re using, so it can apply [[Markdown/Syntax Highlighting|syntax highlighting]]. The block displays the code, it doesn’t run it.

Have a look at [[Markdown]] to learn more about this elegant markup language.

### Development > Server vs. client

## Server vs. client
SilverBullet has two halves you rebuild **independently** — knowing which one you changed saves time:

* The **server** (Rust: `server/`, `server-common/`, `server-runtime-chrome/`, `bin/silverbullet/`) is a compiled binary.
* The **client** (TypeScript: `client/`) is built by ESBuild into `client_bundle/`, which the server serves.

Run the server in development with `cargo run`. A **debug** build serves the client bundle **live from `client_bundle/` on disk** (a release build embeds it). Use `SB_DISABLE_SERVICE_WORKER=1` so the service worker doesn’t cache stale assets:

```shell
SB_DISABLE_SERVICE_WORKER=1 cargo run -p silverbullet -- <PATH-TO-YOUR-DATA-FOLDER>
```

To pass arguments like `-p` or `-L`, put them after `--`:

```shell
SB_DISABLE_SERVICE_WORKER=1 cargo run -p silverbullet -- -L 0.0.0.0 <PATH-TO-YOUR-DATA-FOLDER>
```

**When you change the server** (any Rust code): rebuild **and restart** it — stop the process and re-run `cargo run` (it recompiles). A running server does *not* pick up source changes.

**When you change only the client** (TypeScript in `client/`): you do **not** need to restart the server. Rebuild just the client and reload the page in your browser — the debug server serves the new bundle from disk:

```shell
npm run build:client   # rebuild only the client; then reload the page
```

(For plugs, use `npm run build:plugs`. `npm run build` builds both.)

### TLS (https) > Don’t buffer the event stream

## Don’t buffer the event stream
SilverBullet keeps a server-sent events stream open at `/.events` for live updates. The server sends a ping on it every 30 seconds. If your reverse proxy buffers or compresses this stream, those pings never reach the browser. Live updates then fall back to polling, and stale streams can pile up in the browser and hold connections open.

* **Caddy** passes event streams through unbuffered, so the configuration above needs no changes. If you added an `encode` directive, make sure it doesn’t apply to `text/event-stream`.
* **nginx**: add a location for `/.events` next to your existing one, with buffering and compression turned off:

  ```
  location /.events {
      proxy_pass http://localhost:3000;
      proxy_http_version 1.1;
      proxy_set_header Connection "";
      proxy_set_header Host $host;
      proxy_buffering off;
      proxy_cache off;
      gzip off;
      proxy_read_timeout 1h;
  }
  ```

* **Nginx Proxy Manager**: edit the proxy host, open the _Advanced_ tab and paste the same block, with `proxy_pass $forward_scheme://$server:$port;` so it uses the host’s forward settings.

### TLS (https) > Enable HTTP/2 on your reverse proxy

## Enable HTTP/2 on your reverse proxy
Whichever reverse proxy you use, make sure it serves SilverBullet over HTTP/2. Over HTTP/1.1, browsers allow only six simultaneous connections per host, and SilverBullet’s service worker and sync engine can use all of them. When that happens, every request stalls: the client reports “Could not reach remote server, we’re offline or the server is down”, requests to `/.ping` time out, and pages load slowly from the local copy, even though the server itself is up.

* **Caddy** enables HTTP/2 by default, so the configuration above needs no changes.
* **nginx**: add `http2 on;` to the `server` block (nginx 1.25.1 and later), or use `listen 443 ssl http2;` on older versions.
* **Nginx Proxy Manager**: edit the proxy host, open the _SSL_ tab and enable _HTTP/2 Support_.

To check, run the following, which should print `2`:

```shell
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://silverbullet.mydomain.com/.ping
```

### Schema > Where schemas are saved

## Where schemas are saved
The Data tab saves to its own block in your [[CONFIG]], marked `-- managed-by: workbench-schemas`, next to the block the [[Workbench/Configuration|Configuration]] tab keeps. It's ordinary [[Space Lua]] you can read and edit:

* A schema created here is a `tag.define`.
* Changes to a schema defined elsewhere, such as adding an attribute to `page` or to a library's tag, are kept as separate `config.set` and `tag.setRequired` calls. The original definition is left alone, so later changes to it still take effect.

The block runs after the built-in tags and your other scripts (`-- priority: -10`). When a script that runs even later replaces a schema, saving says which of your changes it overrides.
